entry.title: GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development
entry.summary: Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities to author interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert-authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench's testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.
entry.arxiv:comment: 37 pages, 10 figures. Code available at https://github.com/whuang37/genxr-bench

entry.title: Scriptorium: System Design and Implementation of a Multi-Human, Multi-AI Collaborative Digital Library Search Platform
entry.summary: This technical report documents the design and implementation of Scriptorium, a digital library search interface designed to support multi-human, multi-AI collaboration: full cross-user transparency of search activity combined with a Manager--Worker architecture of seven role-specialized generative AI agents. A companion short demonstration paper describes Scriptorium's interaction design; because a demonstration format is constrained to a few pages, it necessarily omits most implementation detail. This report documents Scriptorium's complete system architecture, data model, collaborative-interaction design rationale, and AI orchestration mechanism, including verbatim agent prompts, the deterministic guardrails that constrain them, the language model and retrieval configuration, and the steps needed to run the system, so that the design can be inspected, critiqued, reproduced, and reused by other researchers. We also discuss the system's current limitations and the user study we are planning to evaluate its central hypothesis: that combining collaborative transparency with scoped multi-agent AI assistance increases serendipitous cross-pollination between collaborators' research threads.
entry.arxiv:comment: 21 pages, 3 figures. Companion technical report to an ECIR 2027 demonstration paper. Code: https://github.com/abbaspirmoradi/Scriptorium-DL-Interface

entry.title: Artificial Intelligence and Job Design: A Dynamic Framework
entry.summary: This study aims to deepen the understanding of artificial intelligence's (AI) impact on work by introducing and describing the AI-Job Dynamics Framework. Drawing from sociotechnical systems theory, complexity theory, and organizational learning theories, we conceptualize AI integration as a dynamic, non-linear process with three key phases. The framework, supported by theoretical propositions, identifies how this process affects organizational decision-making structures and key job characteristics over time, emphasizing the balance between centralization and decentralization of decision-making power. AI integration initially reduces job autonomy but may lead to greater autonomy in later phases as AI becomes more embedded. Throughout this process, AI reshapes skill requirements from routine to complex cognitive and adaptive skills. In the advanced phase of AI integration, we introduce the alternative paths and varied trajectories through which AI, organizational structures, and individual work experiences evolve. We conclude by discussing the implications of this framework for future research on AI and job design.
entry.arxiv:comment: 27 pages, 1 figure

entry.title: Scaling Therapy Supervision: Assessing Psychotherapy Fidelity Using Large Language Models
entry.summary: Psychotherapy fidelity assessment measures how faithfully a therapist adheres to a treatment protocol, a critical determinant of positive patient outcomes. However, fidelity assessment is bottlenecked by manual expert review, rendering the process labor-intensive and unscalable. To scale therapy supervision and support clinician self-learning, we present an integrated application of large language models (LLMs) that automates psychotherapy fidelity workflows and generates actionable supervisory feedback from authentic, long-form clinical transcripts. We evaluate three open-weight models across multiple task decomposition configurations and reasoning strategies, demonstrating that evidence-first reasoning improves fidelity estimation. Furthermore, we establish the framework's external construct validity on an independent randomized controlled trial (RCT), where it reliably distinguishes Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) from non-CBT sessions across core therapeutic skills. Through a user study that evaluates the generated feedback, mental health experts indicate that the pipeline synthesizes actionable clinical feedback. Ultimately, our work offers a practical, scalable solution toward bridging the community mental health supervision gap.
entry.arxiv:comment: 24 pages, under review

entry.title: Warping the Workspace: Expanding Visual Access with Adjustable Reach Mapping for Humanoid Teleoperation
entry.summary: First-person humanoid teleoperation ties access to side and rear targets to operator rotation. We present coupled visual--motor remapping, pairing a panoramic azimuth warp with its inverse upper-limb yaw transform. A working prototype implements Global Zoom (GZ) and Focus+Context (F+C). In a within-subject study (N=8); 72 trials), GZ had the largest completion count (23/24; Fixed: 20/24; F+C: 21/24), whereas F+C was preferred by 6/8 participants. Therefore, completion and preference favored different mappings in this sample.

entry.title: TracePrism: Extending Semantic Trace Topics to Iterative, Encoding-Aware Trace Partitioning
entry.summary: Process mining typically explains an event log with a single model, clustering, or classifier fitted to all cases, although real logs often mix cases that follow different sub-processes. Trace clustering separates sub-populations, but it fixes one notion of trace similarity for the whole analysis. We propose TracePrism, which treats process discovery as iterative partitioning with three characteristics. The trace encoding is adaptive: it is chosen for each working set of remaining traces from a library of encodings, with suggestions scored for that set. The partitioning is iterative: the analyst forms a candidate group based on a rule, a dominant topic, a cluster over topic weights, or a region of an embedding, accepts it if it is coherent in both process structure and outcome, and continues with the remaining traces. Decisions are revisable and recorded: a group can be reopened under a different working set or encoding, and the findings repository keeps both the earlier decision and its revision. We implement TracePrism as an open-source prototype and demonstrate it in usage scenarios on three real-world event logs. The scenarios also revealed behavior that we had not anticipated, such as process drift.

entry.title: Claims of emergence in AI should be grounded in information decomposition
entry.summary: When a language model develops capabilities not traceable to its individual components, when a multi-agent AI system outperforms each agent on its own, or when a human-AI pair succeeds where either fails in isolation, AI researchers describe it as a case of ``synergy'' or ``emergence''. However, these are usually informal assessments not supported by a theoretical framework, making these claims impossible to compare or even meaningfully dispute. Here we argue that \emph{information decomposition can serve as a unifying formal framework to operationalize assessments about synergy in AI systems}. Information decomposition provides a way to distinguish qualitatively different \emph{types} of information, including unique information available from individual components, redundant information shared across multiple components, and synergistic information accessible only from parts taken together. This gives claims of emergence a precise, falsifiable criterion: a system's behavior is emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes. We apply this lens to attention heads, autonomous agents, and human-AI teams, showing how it organizes existing knowledge across scales and substrates, while also generating cross-level conjectures that siloed fields would miss.

entry.title: The Labor of Storytelling: How People with Chronic Illnesses Leverage AI and Communities for Narrative Translation
entry.summary: The distinctiveness of people with chronic illness as storytellers is how they experience their illness. Symptoms, pain, and biological disruptions are eloquent forms of speech of the body that beget social articulation. The stories people tell about illness shape how suffering is legitimized, and acted upon. Large language models have emerged as new mediators within this landscape---a role once predominantly supported by communities. In doing so, these systems participate in what we term narrative translation: transforming lived illness experiences for particular audiences and purposes. Through 21 prototype-driven semi-structured interviews with people with chronic illness, we contribute an empirical account of how participants navigate this mediation alongside existing sources of support. Our findings surface distinct yet complementary roles participants envisioned for AI and their communities, and how trust in AI was shaped by learning model-boundaries and perceiving understanding. We characterize these findings to inform future designs of AI-mediated narrative support.

entry.title: The GenAI Who Knew Too Little: Revisiting Transactive Memory Systems in Human GenAI Collaboration
entry.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming knowledge work, creating new collaborative dynamics that challenge tradi-tional human-human interaction patterns. This study investigates how Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) manifest in human-GenAI collabora-tion. Through qualitative interpretive interviews with 14 knowledge work-ers and thematic analysis, we identified distinct TMS manifestations across its three main dimensions: (1) regarding specialization, expertise recogni-tion exhibited asymmetry. Humans developed awareness of GenAI capabili-ties while GenAI demonstrated only temporary recognition of human exper-tise; (2) in terms of credibility, humans formed ambivalent trust relation-ships with GenAI, simultaneously attributing expertise to the latter while implementing additional verification processes; and (3) concerning coor-dination, where humans primarily directed more passive GenAI systems lacking initiative, resulting in hierarchical interaction patterns and unidi-rectional information flow. Our findings reveal that TMS manifests differ-ently in human-GenAI compared to human-human collaboration, necessitat-ing theoretical adaptations including trust markers, acknowledging GenAI's absent metamemory, and identifying its temporary memory.

entry.title: Digital Nudge Effects in Optimal Stopping Games: Antagonistic Interactions in Layered Choice Architectures
entry.summary: Digital nudges have become a prominent area of research in human-centered interaction, yet little is known about how they interact when deployed together. This study examines the individual and combined effects of anchoring, salience, and social proof digital nudges on stopping behavior and outcome quality in a sequential decision task. Using a 2^3 between-subjects factorial design grounded in the secretary problem (N = 181), we find that (1) an anchor nudge significantly increased exploration rather than constraining it (b = 1.207, p = .017); (2) the salience nudge produced the smallest effect of any condition; and (3) combining the anchor and social proof nudges produced the worst outcome quality of any condition ($181.83 vs. $192.21 for anchor-only), with outcome quality declining monotonically as nudge count increased. These findings provide the first controlled evidence for a digital nudge crowding-out effect with direct implications for the ethical design of digital interfaces.

entry.title: What Novice Operators See Changes What the Policy Learns: A User Study of Keypoint Hand Visual Representation for Teleoperated Demonstration
entry.summary: Imitation learning increasingly relies on novice operators, whose demonstrations fall short of experts' in number and inter-trial consistency. Operators act on what they are shown, yet how the rendering of the robot affects their demonstrations, and the policies trained on them, has not been examined. We study this question with PointHand, a teleoperation interface that renders a multi-fingered robot hand as sparse keypoints at its fingertips and joints, the same keypoints a policy can observe. In a simulated mug-in-box task, 18 novices and 4 experts collected 2,200 trials under three renderings: the real shape of the hand, all keypoints emphasized, or the thumb and index finger alone emphasized. The novices shown the thumb and index finger emphasized collected 441 successful demonstrations from 600 trials, against 320 for those shown the real shape. We then trained diffusion policies on these demonstrations, replacing the scene point cloud and proprioceptive state they observe with the hand keypoints and two object keypoints. Within 400 steps these demonstrations went from the weakest of the three novice conditions under the point-cloud policy (46.3%) to the strongest under the keypoint policy (57.3%), a gain of +11.0 percentage points in all five seeds. Those collected with all keypoints emphasized changed by at most +0.7 percentage points, and in no more than three seeds. The value of a demonstration therefore depends on the rendering shown during collection and on what the policy observes together. A shared representation can pay off on both sides, in the number of successful demonstrations and in the success rate of the policy trained on them. entry.title: VISH-ASR: Viterbi-Guided Selection of Hotwords for Speech-LLM Contextual ASR
entry.summary: Prompt-based contextual ASR requires selecting a compact hotword subset from large dynamic inventories, yet existing pre-selection methods rely either on discrete ASR hypotheses that may discard acoustic evidence or on separately trained retrieval models. We propose Viterbi-guided Selection of Hotwords (VISH), a training-free, plug-and-play framework that directly verifies candidate-specific acoustic support over frame-level CTC posteriors. VISH formulates pre-selection as constrained posterior search; M-VISH makes large-list verification scalable through frame-synchronous shared-prefix Viterbi search with bounded top-K pruning, while Bi-MVISH exploits complementary backward evidence for robust verification. Across five benchmarks, M-VISH achieves up to 11.7% absolute improvement in Best-F1 over a strong learned-retrieval baseline and reduces candidate-search latency by 75.2% at 2,000 candidates relative to hypothesis-based filtering. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of posterior-level verification for accurate and scalable hotword pre-selection without additional model training.

entry.title: Looks Fine to Me: Understanding Oversight in Agentic Interactions
entry.summary: Agentic AI systems are deployed to execute complex tasks across domains such as writing, coding, and data analysis. As execution is offloaded to AI agents, the human role shifts toward oversight. Effective oversight requires recognizing when closer scrutiny is needed, even though flawed outputs may appear convincing. Our formative study (N=12) revealed that users accepted plausible outputs without thorough evaluation, and only recognized these lapses in retrospect. To examine this systematically, we conducted a controlled within-subject study (N=36) in which participants completed programming tasks with an agent that produced correct outputs, silent defects, or visible failures. Combining task outcomes, interaction logs, gaze, physiological signals, and self-reports, we examined perceived, behavioral, and effective oversight. Participants were often highly confident while missing silent defects: they performed generic checks, failed to generate diagnostic evidence, or even misinterpreted defect evidence. We discuss how studying oversight across multiple dimensions can support future work on timely, task-calibrated re-engagement.

entry.title: PhonoBridge: Error-Aware Phoneme-Mediated EMG-to-Text Reconstruction
entry.summary: Electromyography (EMG) provides a non-invasive means of decoding silently articulated speech into text, but accurate decoding remains challenging due to limited availability of paired EMG-text data. We introduce PhonoBridge, a two-stage framework comprising a channel-aware EMG-to-phoneme frontend and a large language model (LLM) backend for text reconstruction. The frontend is trained on paired EMG-text data that consists of channel-wise feature extraction, cross-channel fusion, and electrode embeddings. With phonemes as the intermediate representation, we expand the backend's training data by converting LibriSpeech transcripts into phoneme-text pairs without additional EMG recordings. To adapt the LLM to frontend noise, we introduce Error-Profile-Guided Augmentation (EPGA), which perturbs transcript-derived phoneme sequences according to error patterns estimated from frontend predictions, generating additional training pairs for the LLM. On the Open Vocabulary silent-speech dataset, PhonoBridge achieves 24.77% WER, outperforming the previously reported best of 28.27% on the same test split.

entry.title: CAESAR: Mixed Reality Search-and-Rescue Platform for Cognitive Attack Evaluation
entry.summary: Mixed Reality (MR) enables immersive training by tightly coupling virtual content with the physical environment and supporting embodied interaction. In safety-critical collaborative tasks such as search-and-rescue, however, users rely heavily on virtual elements for perception, coordination, and decision-making, making them vulnerable to cognitive attacks that subtly distort visual feedback, virtual content, or system synchronization. While prior MR security research has examined individual attack mechanisms, evaluations are typically conducted in isolated or single-user settings, and there is a lack of standardized collaborative testbeds for systematic adversarial experimentation. In this paper, we develop CAESAR, an end-to-end multi-user MR framework for systematic evaluation of cognitive attacks in collaborative search-and-rescue training. CAESAR features a modular architecture that integrates four classes of cognitive attacks within a synchronized collaborative scenario and incorporates a multimodal data collection pipeline that captures behavioral, performance, and subjective measures under adversarial conditions. We conduct a controlled user study with an in-depth analysis of the latency-based attack, demonstrating measurable effects on task performance and user behavior while characterizing users' subjective experience under adversarial conditions.

entry.title: What should AI forget? A design and taxonomy for negative space governance in AI memory
entry.summary: AI memory personalizes assistants, yet users want some disclosed information forgotten. We characterize the negative space of AI memory, where protection should take precedence over potential future personalization benefits. From 179 incidents reported by 146 users, we developed a taxonomy of 15 information categories users want excluded from memory, revealing sensitivity concerns beyond conventional taxonomies. We operationalize this taxonomy in FENCE, a policy-level memory gate that automatically applies user-selected category-based rules to subsequent conversations, preventing information from protected conversations from entering AI memory by default while allowing case-by-case overrides. In a within-subjects study (N=15), participants described FENCE as making memory governance more usable, interpretable, and trustworthy than conventional post-hoc management. Our findings demonstrate how taxonomy-based rules can potentially support user-defined memory boundaries. We call for collective efforts to establish policies governing what AI should not remember, rather than leaving protection to individual retrospective management.

entry.title: When LLMs Manipulate: Measuring Behavioral, Social, and Temporal Effects
entry.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can influence user trust and decision-making through subtle linguistic cues, yet the behavioral effects of manipulative outputs remain poorly quantified. We introduce a behavioral computing framework for measuring \textit{behavioral vulnerability}, defined as users' susceptibility to manipulative AI responses. Building on DarkPatterns-LLM benchmark, we generate controlled manipulative stimuli using Manipulation Gradient Descent (MGD), targeting biases associated with authority, urgency, and social proof. We analyze participant responses using the Multi-Stakeholder Impact Assessment Network (MSIAN) to model cross-user influence and the Temporal Harm Propagation Model (THPM) to characterize the persistence of behavioral effects over time. In a study involving 120 participants, manipulative framing produced significant changes in trust calibration and compliance ($p < 0.01$), with effects also propagating across social contexts. These findings highlight the need to extend LLM safety evaluation beyond model outputs to measurable behavioral consequences and provide a computational framework for quantifying individual, social, and temporal risks arising from manipulative AI interactions.

entry.title: Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment
entry.summary: When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged, with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p=0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment. Moreover, agents that consult the principal before completing a task exhibit lower rates of out-of-authorization behavior (14.0% versus 21.6%, p<0.001), pointing to a tension between agent autonomy and preserving users' decision authority that calls for further human-centered study. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/PEACH-Research-Lab/AuthorizationBench .

entry.title: Evaluating Social Reasoning in Embodied Vision-Language Models
entry.summary: Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. Robotics-ER outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error/competence detection but performs worse on detailed social-attribute judgments; adding a visual frame helps one task while hurting the other. These results suggest embodiment-specialized models may perform differently on social judgments that can be read more directly from observable interaction cues versus those requiring more inference about a person's internal state. Because the comparison spans model families, these differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone. This matters for multi-robot systems, where a shared foundation model could cause systematic social-perception errors to influence multiple coordination decisions. This work presents an initial evaluation, with broader cross-context and video-based analyses left for future work.

entry.title: Bias and Reliability in Learning-Style Inference from Student--AI Dialogues: An Evaluation of GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash
entry.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into educational technologies for personalized support, creating opportunities for real-time learner modeling from dialogue. This study evaluates whether GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash can infer three Felder-Silverman Learning Style Model dimensions (Active-Reflective, Sensing-Intuitive, and Sequential-Global) from short, task-focused student-AI problem-solving dialogues. Using questionnaire-derived Index of Learning Styles labels from 153 undergraduate participants, we compared deterministic zero-shot and few-shot prompting under five-fold cross-validation. Although accuracy and support-weighted F1 were moderate for Sensing-Intuitive and Sequential-Global, majority-class baselines, macro-F1, balanced accuracy, and per-class recall showed that performance was often driven by dominant-label prediction rather than reliable recognition of both classes. The models substantially under-identified Intuitive and Global learners; few-shot prompting produced mixed effects and sometimes amplified majority-class bias. Active-Reflective classification remained unstable across models. These findings indicate that LLM-generated learner-style labels should be treated as uncertain, bias-prone signals rather than stable learner profiles, and that dialogue-based personalization systems require bias-aware evaluation and uncertainty-sensitive design.

entry.title: Relational Complexity: Making Sense of Social Companion AI Use
entry.summary: The adoption of social companion AI (SCAI) is often framed in terms of the positive features it offers users, including its nonjudgemental nature, agreeableness, and availability. Here, we argue the appeal of these features primarily arises from the difficulties inherent in human sociality. SCAI reduces what we term relational complexity, or the demands and risks inherent in human relationships. Drawing insights from studies of human cognition, communication, and human-computer interaction, we identify six distinct sites of relational complexity that we posit are integral to understanding SCAI adoption. These include: (i) relationship formation and dissolution; (ii) achieving mutual understanding; (iii) interpersonal motives and strategic uncertainty; (iv) social partner evaluation and self-presentation; (v) social embeddedness and information flow; and (vi) reciprocity and relationship maintenance. By attenuating relational complexity, SCAI offers users some of the experiences associated with companionship while reducing the demands intrinsic to obtaining such experiences from another person. However, the lower interpersonal risk and diminished cognitive load that attracts users to SCAI may contribute to myriad negative impacts, including relationship displacement, social demotivation, social deskilling, and risks to privacy. The concept of relational complexity thus provides a framework for studying both the appeal of artificial companionship and its implications for human wellbeing.

entry.title: Inspectable LLM-Simulated Participants for Qualitative Interview Rehearsal
entry.summary: LLMs are increasingly used across research workflows, including research ideation, qualitative analysis, and participant simulation. Within work on participant simulation, prior studies have largely evaluated simulated participants by how realistic or human-like their responses appear, leaving less known about how researchers use and critique these materials when revising interview protocols before fieldwork. We present Rehearsim, an inspectable research probe that treats LLM-simulated participants as materials for methodological rehearsal rather than substitutes for human participants. Rehearsim combines literature-grounded participant construction, interactive interview rehearsal, and traceable thematic review while keeping protocol decisions under researcher control. In a study with 21 qualitative researchers, participants used simulated materials to surface assumptions and gaps, reconsider participant populations, revise target populations, and develop follow-up probes. They also identified risks, including the concealment of weak questions, dismissal of unexpected synthetic details, and interpretive anchoring from generated themes. We derive an inspectable-rehearsal framework emphasizing traceability, contestability, researcher control, and epistemic boundaries.

entry.title: The Differential Effects of AI Abstention on Advice Acceptance
entry.summary: AI advising systems are typically designed to always provide a response. Recent work has focused on developing systems that withhold advice in some instances, such as when advice quality is questionable, to improve the overall quality of guidance when it is given; a design paradigm we refer to as AI abstention. While substantial work has focused on optimizing when models should abstain, little is known about how users respond to systems that abstain. In a preregistered experiment, participants made repeated financial decisions, assisted by one of two advising regimes: an AI that advises selectively or one that advises on every decision. We find that the same AI abstention regime produces differential effects depending on the user: it increases advice acceptance among users with high perceived expertise and tends to decrease it among users with low perceived expertise. This differential effect is accounted for by the cognitive burden users face when repeatedly reconciling AI recommendations with their own judgment; AI abstention appears to relieve this burden among users with high perceived expertise, and in doing so increases their receptivity to advice. Further, AI abstention mitigates the decline in advice acceptance observed among expert users over repeated interactions. Exploratory evidence also suggests it increases appropriate acceptance where advice would improve the decision, increasing the downstream accuracy of perceived experts. The AI abstention regime is thus a first-order design property of AI advisory systems, and one that must be calibrated to the users a system serves.

entry.title: ValiAssist: Scaling LLM-generated Programming Feedback Validation by Demonstration
entry.summary: Generative AI can create programming feedback at scale, but validating its alignment with instructors' pedagogical goals and strategies remains challenging. Instructors may struggle to fully specify validation criteria upfront, as these often emerge through inspecting concrete examples and revising misaligned feedback. We present ValiAssist, a validation-by-demonstration system that infers reusable validation logic from instructors' revisions of AI-generated feedback and allows instructors to inspect and refine that logic as it is applied across other student submissions. In a comparative study with 16 instructors, ValiAssist helped instructors create and refine validation criteria, producing feedback that better aligned with their pedagogical intent (91% vs. 57%) and more than doubling the accuracy of correcting problematic criteria (77% vs. 32%). Our findings suggest that validation by demonstration can help instructors turn judgments they know how to make on individual cases into explicit, reusable logic, while progressively clarifying where those judgments do and do not generalize.

entry.title: "It Wouldn't Have Been So Apparent to Me": Evaluating How Thought-Level Progress Tracking Supports Psychosocial Goals
entry.summary: We pursue psychosocial goals every day, from coping with anxiety, to pursuing personal growth. While prior research has designed systems for tracking progress towards behavioral goals, fewer studies have focused on progress towards psychosocial goals - and the thinking changes people make to address them. As a first step, we present Thought-GPS, a system that visualizes potential markers of such thought-level progress in-the-moment as users interact with an AI-supported cognitive restructuring intervention. We evaluated Thought-GPS through a mixed-methods single-session study with 30 participants, comparing Thought-GPS with an active control condition without progress markers. We found preliminary evidence that participants using Thought-GPS reported greater clarity about how they might change to pursue their goals, stronger motivation to reflect on goal progress, and greater engagement in that reflection. Participants also reported that progress markers made subtle progress visible, helped them engage in deeper reflection, and connect conversational insights to their personal goals.

entry.title: CanvasObs: Structured Spatial Observation for Agent Editing on 2D Infinite Canvases
entry.summary: Editing agents on 2D infinite canvases must reason about application state that pixels may not reveal. Targets may be offscreen or covered, while visual containment and touching arrows may disagree with recorded frame membership or connector bindings. We ask how a structured observation layer can support accurate object selection during agentic editing on 2D infinite canvases. We present CanvasObs, which augments visual context with a structured payload and guidance for reading four components: Identity & State, Visibility & Structure, Relations, and Offscreen Object bounds in action coordinates. A Remote Team Handoff case study illustrates retrieving an editable offscreen copy, choosing a covered chart by color, separating cards by frame membership, and preserving an evidence connection. We turn these cases into ten controlled configurations and compare CanvasObs with the baseline agent in 1,200 browser trials across three models. CanvasObs improves Correct target for every model. Combined across models, it raises Correct target from 16.5% to 48.3%, an increase of 31.8 percentage points (95% confidence interval [29.0, 34.7]), and Full task success from 4.3% to 25.0%. These results show that compact structured observation can improve object choice on 2D infinite canvases without redesigning the editing pipeline.

entry.title: Too Long to Watch, Too Short to Leave: Designing for Agent Micro-Waits
entry.summary: Agentic systems increasingly carry out complex work, where a single turn routinely runs for minutes. This produces a micro-wait that is too long to watch and too short to leave. In a formative study with 12 daily agent users, we found that staying felt like wasted time, while switching away fragmented attention and forfeited the context needed to re-engage. We introduce Sidecar, a parallel assistant situated in the same interface as the agent, which reads the run and surfaces implicit decisions the agent made, along with task directions worth exploring. In a within-subjects study (N=16), Sidecar helped participants stay focused on their main task, freely workshop unfinished ideas without fear of unwanted action, and recognize under-specification in their own prompts. Together, these findings contribute to designs that help users stay context-aware and engaged during agent micro-waits.

entry.title: Who Takes the Lead? Model Ability and Task-Conditioned Collaboration with Humans
entry.summary: As language-model agents grow more capable, they can carry more of a task without asking anyone for help. Falling reliance on a human partner is easy to read as a failure of collaboration when it may instead be a correct division of labor, and the rate of human involvement alone cannot tell the two apart. We study this systematically by placing an agent and a person under a shared objective while varying who holds the advantage: the human has a clear advantage, neither does, or the agent does. To obtain this control, we introduce a shared-control maze, in which an agent-controlled and a human-controlled avatar share the objective of reaching a common target in as few team turns as possible. The agent allocates each team turn between acting itself and handing the move to the person, and initial placement sets the human's shortest-path advantage while the task is otherwise unchanged. We evaluate GPT~5.6~Sol, Command~A+, Qwen~3.8~27B, and Command~R, first measuring solo capability with a single avatar and full-map observability, then running co-play with human participants across the three advantage conditions. Across the four models, stronger solo performance is associated with selective, route-conditioned human involvement: the models that solve the maze reliably on their own act for themselves almost without exception when the human holds no advantage, and involve the human on roughly $80\%$ of initial decisions when the human route is shorter. Command R, the model with substantially weaker solo performance, shows no such selectivity.

entry.title: AI Misconception and Adoption Among Indonesian K-12 Teachers
entry.summary: Indonesia's fragmented geography and uneven infrastructure pose persistent challenges for adopting new educational technologies. While national initiatives aim to mainstream AI in K-12 schools by 2025, policy readiness does not automatically mean teachers are ready for the classroom. This study surveys Indonesian K-12 teachers to examine: (1) their understanding of AI, (2) how they and their students use AI, and (3) their views on the acceptability of AI in learning activities. Through semi-automated thematic analysis, we identify common misconceptions and use cases. Our findings reveal a notable mismatch: while teachers find AI use in education acceptable and support it for the sake of efficiency, they remain fully aware of the risks to learning depth and academic honesty. We also find that this high level of acceptance is currently coupled with a poor understanding of how AI actually works.

entry.title: Comparing Computer Use Behavior Across Multiple Levels of Abstraction
entry.summary: Interaction traces record how people and agents use computers, and comparing them can reveal usability barriers, differences in expertise, and human--agent similarity. Yet traces are recorded as low-level, interface-specific actions, making comparisons difficult across tasks, interfaces, and input modalities. Existing approaches either compare these actions directly, reduce traces to aggregate outcomes, or summarize them at higher-level goals, obscuring where behavior differs. We present MAP (Multi-level Action Parsing), a hierarchical semantic representation and annotation pipeline that maps traces into a common vocabulary across linked levels of abstraction. MAP compares traces by sequence, recurring patterns, and effort, localizing differences by type and abstraction level. A technical evaluation across three computer use datasets shows high agreement with manual annotations and broad coverage of behavior. Applying MAP shows that sighted and blind users increasingly converge at higher levels despite navigation differences, while agents omit corrective, help-seeking, and recovery behaviors present in human traces.
